name: Cetirizine and antihistamines
summary: A second-generation (less sedating) antihistamine that blocks histamine H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and other allergic symptoms. It works within about an hour, is taken once a day and is sold without prescription, but it is the most sedating of the modern antihistamines and is an add-on, never a substitute for adrenaline, in anaphylaxis.
usedFor: Hay fever and year-round allergic rhinitis: sneezing, runny nose, itchy or watery eyes; also allergic conjunctivitis
Urticaria (hives), itching and the itch of eczema
Mild allergic reactions to foods, insect bites and drugs (not a substitute for adrenaline in anaphylaxis)
Sedating first-generation antihistamines (chlorphenamine, promethazine) for short-term itch or nausea
howItWorks: Blocks H1 histamine receptors on blood vessels, nerves and smooth muscle. When mast cells release histamine in response to an allergen, it normally makes capillaries leak (swelling, runny nose), stimulates itch nerves and constricts airways; with the receptors occupied, those effects are muted. Second-generation drugs cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so they cause much less drowsiness than older ones. The NHS puts it this way: on contact with something a person is allergic to, such as pollen or animal fur, the body produces histamine, and cetirizine works by blocking its effects, so symptoms begin to ease within an hour. It treats the symptoms rather than the allergy itself, so it is taken for as long as exposure continues (a pollen season, a flare of hives) and can be used daily over long periods. Among the non-sedating antihistamines, cetirizine is the one most likely to cause sleepiness; loratadine, desloratadine and fexofenadine are less so, which guides the choice for drivers and shift workers. Cetirizine also exists as eye drops for itchy allergic conjunctivitis and, in some countries, as an intravenous injection for acute hives given by a healthcare professional.
onset: Within an hour; lasts 24 hours, so it is taken once a day.

common: Feeling sleepy or tired is the most common effect (more than 1 in 10 people, and more than with loratadine, desloratadine or fexofenadine)
Headache, dry mouth, feeling sick, dizziness, diarrhoea; getting up slowly helps dizziness, and driving, cycling or using machinery is avoided while dizzy or drowsy
Severe or prolonged diarrhoea or vomiting can reduce the protection of contraceptive pills
serious: Rare serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to the medicine itself: sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue needs an emergency (999) call
Unusual bruising or bleeding that is slow to stop, which the NHS advises reporting to a doctor or NHS 111
Marked sedation and impaired driving with first-generation agents; confusion and falls in the elderly, urinary retention in men with prostate enlargement
QT prolongation with some older non-sedating agents (withdrawn)
Severe itching on stopping suddenly after long regular use (a very small risk, so a doctor is consulted before stopping long-term daily treatment)

cautions: Check driving response with any antihistamine; avoid or limit alcohol, which adds to the drowsiness
Dose reduced in kidney impairment for cetirizine
Not for children under 2 without advice; sedating antihistamines avoided in young children
Anaphylaxis needs adrenaline first: antihistamines are adjuncts only
Long-term daily use is regarded as safe, but the NHS advises using it only for as long as it is needed and checking with a doctor before stopping after prolonged regular use
monitoring: None. No blood tests are needed; the only follow-up is checking that symptoms are controlled and that drowsiness is not interfering with driving, work or school, and reviewing whether the medicine is still needed once the allergen exposure has passed.
